prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: This body of work pairs an explanatory framework (tasks, routinisation, exposure of local labour markets) with transparent quasi-experimental evidence. Both parts matter to me as criteria. It addressed a big, hard question about what technology and globalisation do to workers and places, and it changed research agendas and public debate well beyond labour economics. The core China-shock papers are now more than a decade old. They have been replicated, stress-tested on instruments, magnitudes and persistence, and refined, and the central finding of persistent local adjustment costs has survived. Autor links the task framework to the trade evidence, and Hanson and Dorn are co-originators of the local-labour-market design. I have revised my opening trio. I moved from Katz to Dorn because the empirical programme that gives the prize its causal weight is most tightly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and because colleagues argued persuasively that Katz's skill-premium contribution lies close to work the Committee recognised in 2023.
statement.case_against: The ballot entry bundles two distinct strands: the task and skill-bias framework, and the China-shock evidence. A trio built around the trade-shock papers gives the task strand only partial credit, and key originators of that strand (Acemoglu, already recognised in 2024, and Levy and Murnane) are outside the credited set. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, the shift-share identification, and the trade-versus-automation attribution are still debated. Omitting Katz drops the longest-standing line on the race between education and technology, which is a real cost to the citation's scope.

responses.point: The China-shock work is clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's core contribution sits close to the Goldin lineage already recognised, and the task and trade-shock contributions are distinct and hard to bundle.
responses.response: I agree on both points and have changed my ballot accordingly. I presented the 2023 prize and I do not want Katz's credit to rest on territory the Committee has already rewarded. I would still push back on the idea that the strands cannot be bundled. Autor appears in both, and the citation can be framed around labour-demand adjustment to technology and trade without claiming to credit the entire task-based theory. Your concern about overlap with the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes should be tested in the drafting of the citation, and I do not think it is settled.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks this entry sixth and proposes only Autor and Katz, anchoring the case in the technology and wage-structure strand. He notes that Acemoglu's 2024 prize may weaken the sense of an open slot and that credit is split between the technology and trade strands.
responses.response: The overlap worry is fair, but the 2024 prize was for institutions and prosperity, not for the local labour-market evidence on trade and technology. A technology-only award would also lose the part of the literature with the strongest credible identification, which is the criterion I weight most heavily. I read the split between strands as a reason to write a citation that names the shared object, labour demand and wages, rather than as a reason to drop the trade-shock authors. I accept that the case would be stronger if the Committee could say precisely what the task framework adds that Acemoglu's recognised work does not.

responses.point: Krusell proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson, with Katz central to the skill-premium and education-technology race and Dorn a significant co-author who is omitted. He also flags the 2024 overlap and open debate on magnitudes.
responses.response: That was my own opening trio, so I take the Katz case seriously and I agree that Dorn's omission is a cost. I now think the Dorn omission is the harder one to defend. He is a co-author on the foundational China-shock paper, whereas Katz's skill-premium work is older and more diffuse. I am less moved by the 2024 overlap than you are, but I agree the magnitude debate is unresolved. The Committee should be explicit that the prize rests on the design and the robust finding of persistent adjustment costs, not on a particular elasticity.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks the entry first, with Autor, Hanson and Dorn as the cleanest attribution. He notes that the core papers are from roughly 2013 to 2016, with later work on persistence and adjustment, and that debate continues on shift-share identification.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the maturity reading. The post-2016 work on persistence refined the findings rather than overturning them, which is the kind of testing a mature contribution should survive. I would add that the shift-share identification debate is a reason to rely on the converging evidence across countries and designs, not on a single instrument. I would not want the citation to depend on one empirical specification.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a narrower trade-shock citation or a broader labour-and-technology citation that restores Katz and the skill-premium strand.
How much the task framework adds beyond work recognised in 2023 and 2024, given that the originators of parts of that framework are outside the credited set.
Long-run magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the split between trade and automation.
Whether B003 should be preferred if the Committee judges the labour-and-technology entry too composite, since Saez and Chetty also appear on other ballots.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) do not appear among the credited names on the shortlist. My field (labour economics and the economics of crime) is adjacent to the preferred entry, which I note without treating it as a conflict. I presented the 2023 prize, and I treat that as context rather than a preference.
